whatItFakes: While the player skips, the character’s own pick (the core’s chooseAct selection) is resumed as a player answer, so the saved act carries a controlled-choice reason key.
why: The core’s player clock has no resume kind that records an act as the character’s own decision. Resolved by OPUS-PLAY (2026-10-12): the bench resumes with OPUS-CORE's own-choice kind (core2-api-v12), so the act is saved as the character's own decision.
replacement: An OPUS-CORE resume kind that saves the act as the character’s own decision while control is held.

whatItFakes: The bench builds a smaller town (2,000 people by default) instead of the full opening cohort.
why: A day of the full 40,000-person town takes about 13 seconds, too slow to play. Resolved by OPUS-PLAY (2026-10-12): /play builds the whole place two-level (OPUS-CORE), and a year runs in 39 s; the developer page's size field is a tool, not a stand-in.
replacement: OPUS-CORE’s two-level population and speed work, after which the bench builds the full place.

whatItFakes: Every home in the bench shows the shared suburban house interior.
why: New-core households record no dwelling type (apartment, mobile home, rowhouse, farmhouse), so the picture cannot follow the home. Resolved by OPUS-PLAY (2026-10-12): the scene reads OPUS-WORLD's dwellingKind (house, rowhouse, apartment, mobile home, farmhouse) and shows that home's picture.
replacement: A dwelling type on each household from OPUS-WORLD housing or OPUS-PEOPLE, read by the bench scene picker.

whatItFakes: Before a door-knocking round, the bench fills in from the counts as many of the town’s households as the round could reach, so the campaign engine has doors to knock in the two-level world.
why: knockDoors walks only the households already in the core; in the two-level world most of the town is counts.
replacement: OPUS-GOV’s knockDoors (with OPUS-CORE’s fillInPerson) filling in each household it actually reaches. Resolved by Second Session D, October 15, 2026: removed bench fillDoors; campaigns.walkDoors already visits both population tiers and knockDoors fills only the household whose adult actually opens.

whatItFakes: Election night names a drawn challenger by repeating the voting module’s private identity draw (same seed, seat key and role).
why: The voting module draws challengers’ identities privately and exports no name reader.
replacement: An OPUS-GOV export that names any candidate id (resident, official term or drawn challenger). Resolved Oct 16, 2026: election night reads candidateIdentity (src/core2/candidate-identity.ts), exported by the voting module, and the bench's own repeat of the draw is deleted.

whatItFakes: Where OPUS-WORDS' mined bank has no name for an act yet (care for a relative, join an association, hold a meeting, visit an office), the play screen names its choice button from a bench table of control names (“Look after”).
why: The mined choice-names bank (data/english/parts/choice-names.json) covers about half the core's acts; a raw action id is not something a player should read.
replacement: Mined names for every act in OPUS-WORDS' bank, composed by OPUS-PEOPLE's English engine; then this table is removed.

whatItFakes: A /play town whose opening has a kin move dated after the opening day opens without the core’s opening economy (retirement income, customers) and outside market, on the finance-only route.
why: OPUS-PEOPLE’s opening kin moves can be dated after the opening day, which the core’s retirement-income step refuses (“Past fact outside recipient lifetime/opening”). Resolved Oct 16, 2026 (core-kin-moves-clamped-to-opening): kin moves are dated no later than the opening day (opening-kin.ts), so no town fails the income check; Valmont, Colorado and 15 other drawn places open on the full economy, and the bench's fallback is deleted.
replacement: Opening kin moves dated on or before the opening day (OPUS-PEOPLE), so every town takes the closures route; then this fallback is removed.

whatItFakes: The bench applies the custom-world settings (wages, household cash, outside demand) with its own copy of the core's arithmetic; lean and turnout are recorded on the world but nothing reads them yet.
why: OPUS-CORE's applyOpeningSettings and scaleOutsideSales aren't exported, and no engine reads the politics settings yet (audit 4).
replacement: OPUS-CORE exports its settings step for any opening; OPUS-PEOPLE (views) and OPUS-GOV (turnout, party strength) read placeMetadata.worldSettings. Resolved by Second Session D, October 15, 2026: both openings import core2/world-settings.ts; removed the bench arithmetic copy. Political settings are read by electorate.customPolitics.

whatItFakes: Dev mode's count of who a law reached reads only the law-effects, law-reach and law raise records that name the law: full people by id, counted people where a record names one or carries a count. A law's effect that leaves no record naming it is not counted.
why: The core's law-reach count across both tiers of the population is being built by OPUS-CORE and has not landed.
replacement: OPUS-CORE's law-reach count function, read by DevMode.reach.

whatItFakes: Dev mode's public-salary base raises every public job paid under it once, through rerateJob and the law-reach teacher floor's daily-pay arithmetic; it is not a standing law, so a public job filled later is not held to it except where the employer's pay for a new hire follows its raised staff.
why: No law series in the catalog sets every public worker's pay; whether a public-salary base is a law at each level or a budget line is the owner's call. Resolved by OPUS-PLAY (2026-10-14): the CTO ruled a public-salary base is a standing law; the public pay floor law series (src/core2/public-pay-floor.ts) replaces the one-time raise, and dev mode's experiment passes that law.
replacement: The owner's ruling: a public-salary-floor law series read by the law-reach engine (OPUS-GOV), generalizing the teacher floor to read the law's value and every public employer, after which the experiment becomes a law step.

whatItFakes: The desktop shell's update dialogs (Check for Updates, and the Mac note on what installing does) are written in the shell, not by the English engine.
why: The shell runs outside the game, where the English engine is not loaded; the owner ordered a plain dialog telling the player what the Mac install does (Oct 14, 2026).
replacement: Shell lines drawn from an English-engine bank shipped beside the client, read by main.mjs.

whatItFakes: The Windows package job (and the Windows build in each release) may fail without failing the checks or blocking the Mac release.
why: Owner's call (Oct 14, 2026): the Mac build is what matters now; Windows can stay red until early access.
replacement: Early-access preparation: the Windows job made green and required again, and every release carrying latest.yml. docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md: 'The Mac package is the one that must pass; the Windows row stays allowed-to-fail until early access.' docs/coordination/BOARD.md: 'Windows may stay red until early access.' The workflow keeps continue-on-error on the Windows row on that ruling.

whatItFakes: New game writes the chosen name, birth date, gender and appearance recipe straight onto the new world's player record from the play handler, instead of through a core API.
why: The new core has no API for setting the player's identity after a world is built; the old creator lived on the retired engine.
replacement: An OPUS-CORE identity call (name, birth date, sex, appearance) that the creator uses and that keeps indexes and records consistent. Resolved Oct 16, 2026: CoreAPI.chooseIdentityV1 (controlled player only, before the first day passes) is what the creator calls; the bench no longer writes person fields.

whatItFakes: Changing the age in the creator moves only the birth date; the life's generated past (schooling, work, household, family ages) stays as it was drawn for the original age.
why: World building draws the player's past during New game, before the creator runs, and there is no step to redraw it for a chosen age.
replacement: New game passes the chosen age and birthday into the world build (or a core redraw of the player's past) so the history matches the age. Resolved Oct 27, 2026: the chosen birthday goes into the world build (buildBenchWorld's playerBirthDate), which holds a resident of that age and makes the player the resident born nearest it, so the household, kin, schooling, work and money drawn for them fit the age; the identity call then sets the name, exact birth date and looks.

whatItFakes: A town the Census Vintage 2025 estimates and the ACS 2020-2024 table hold no count for (34 of 32,508 places, mostly military posts and merged places) opens at the model's own size (targetPopulation), and the creator's list shows that size, marked as an estimate, so the list and the opened world agree.
why: The records name the place but hold no count for it; the creator must show a number (estimate, never unknown) and the real count needs research per place.
replacement: A sourced count for each of the 34 places (Census 2020 decennial or the base's own published figure), after which the estimate branch is deleted.

whatItFakes: An inauguration's address is staged at the House rostrum, in every world, because that is the one national picture with a podium and seats behind it.
why: The inauguration record (inauguration:2025-01-20) carries no venue, and the Capitol steps have no podium in the painted pictures, so the President could not be drawn at a lectern with the Vice President and others behind him at the White House.
replacement: Resolved Oct 28 by deletion: the opening's picture table is gone (trim-main-every-duplicate-deleted, row W1/B1 of docs/reports/duplicates-on-main-2026-10-28.md), so nothing stages the address at the House rostrum. When the address plays as the director's address situation type (director-opening-as-a-scene), its place comes from the scene's own place rule; the inauguration record still carries no venue.

whatItFakes: Every controlled person's day starts at one minute (7:00 AM, playerDayStartMinute): Day, Week and a calendar jump land on it, and the director's scenes at home wait for it, instead of the person's own wake time.
why: The core keeps no wake or sleep time for a person; work shifts start and end, but nothing says when anyone gets up.
replacement: A person's own wake time from their work schedule, household and age (American Time Use Survey sleep and waking hours by age and employment), read by the bench's day driver and the director's openedAt.

whatItFakes: Whether a home's room is drawn tidy, lived-in or rundown is read from the household's third of the town's homes by value or rent, its tenure and its size, because no dwelling record carries a condition.
why: The art session painted lived-in and rundown versions of the home rooms (art/backdrops, Oct 28) and the housing module keeps value, rent and tenure but no repair state.
replacement: A dwelling condition the housing module keeps (repairs, landlord upkeep, age of the building), read here in place of the third.

whatItFakes: Where a room holds more people than its mannequin plate painted (a council's gallery, an election-night crowd, a big household), the old hand-typed spots the plate does not cover stay after the plate's own spots, with their depth masks, instead of measured ones.
why: The plates for the opening rooms paint a few people each (art/people-rooms/spots, Oct 28); the rooms seat more, and dropping the old spots would leave people unplaced.
replacement: A fuller plate for each such room (every seat of the gallery or crowd painted with a mannequin), measured by the art session; the importer then keeps no old spot.

whatItFakes: Which states take a place's regional rebuild (New England, Mountain West, Southwest, Plains, Deep South, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Pacific islands) is a list in data drawn from the Census Bureau's divisions and common usage; states no region names show the plain painting.
why: The art session painted eight regional rebuilds of four places (Oct 28); no record of a place's regional character exists to read.
replacement: Each place's own architectural region in the place records (or a finer list per county), read here in place of the state list.

whatItFakes: Everyone drawn in a room is one of the people pack's six painted adults (a woman and a man, each slim, medium and heavy), each with their own painted skin and face; a child is not drawn, a teen is drawn as one of the adults, and a person is drawn only where a mannequin plate has a spot in a pose the pack paints them in.
why: Pack v3 ships six people (owner, Oct 29: six now, six more faces follow as manifest rows) and five mannequin plates; the CTO adds plates golden path first.
replacement: More people (ages, faces, skin) and more plates as manifest rows and plate files; no code change.

whatItFakes: Pack v4 paints the standard Oval Office poses for some people and not others: the medium and slim men and the heavy woman have no `stand` figure, the heavy man no `couch` figure, and the three women and the heavy man no `gesture` figure. A person without the pose a spot needs is not drawn there and takes another spot, so a President drawn as the medium man sits at the desk but cannot stand behind it, and the heavy man never sits on the Oval Office couches.
why: The art session drew the standard poses for some people first (pack v4 README); the rest follow as manifest rows.
replacement: A `stand`, `couch` and `gesture` figure for every pack person at the five angles, added as manifest rows (pool item people-pack-v4-pose-gaps); no code change.

whatItFakes: Where a person should wear everyday clothes (at home, on the street) but the pack paints no everyday figure for them in the spot's pose, they are drawn in their work clothes instead of being left out of the scene. In the opening home the slim woman sits on the couch in a blazer because the pack has no everyday seated-talking figure for her.
why: A view never drops someone the simulation put in the scene (CTO ruling, Oct 29, on the owner's everyday-and-work-clothes ruling); the pack's everyday kit is painted in fewer poses than the work looks.
replacement: An everyday figure for every pack person in every pose a plate uses (talk and listen on chairs, couch, write at a desk, stand), added as manifest rows; then `dressOrder.everyday` drops its work dresses in data.

whatItFakes: Politics → Government offers Legislative and Executive but no Judicial branch, though the Oct 14 mock and the owner's Oct 29 answer (judges as read-only cards) have one: no judge exists in the world as an office or a person, so the tab would be empty.
why: Courts come after early access (owner, Oct 10), and the justice engine decides cases without judges (SG-WORLD-housing-hearing-without-judge); nothing on screen may do nothing.
replacement: Judges seated in the world as offices with holders (pool item world-judges-seated), then the Judicial tab draws them as read-only member cards through the same member card and pager.

whatItFakes: A household's living room is picked from the rooms of its dwelling's list that have a mannequin plate, when any has one, so every house shows the same plated living room (house-suburban-living) and the other house rooms (suburban-house, large-house, the regional houses) are not shown.
why: People are drawn only on a plate (owner, Oct 28 and 29), and only house-suburban-living of the house living rooms has one; without the preference about a third of opening evenings drew nobody and nobody could be talked to (people-home-plates).
replacement: Plates for every house living room (people-home-plates); once each room the lists name has one, the preference picks from the whole list and is deleted.

whatItFakes: Poll, Mail and Put in your own money are buttons on the campaign trail card in Travel, not scenes at places (donor calls, the volunteer shift, the endorsement meeting and the ad buy became scenes; the Donations button, a twin of Call donors, is gone).
why: The Campaigns tab shows standing only (owner, Oct 20: campaign acts are scenes you go to); the doors, event, forum, interview, calls, donor meeting, speech and debate already start their scenes, and these five have no scene yet.
replacement: Each becomes a scene the director stages (play-campaign-acts-as-scenes): an evening of donor calls, a volunteer shift at the office, an endorsement meeting, an ad shoot, the pollster's briefing, the mail piece, putting in your own money; then the buttons and this entry are deleted.

whatItFakes: A filing office whose clerk has no work record to read (a state's election office, a municipal finance officer who is not one of the town's full people) keeps assumed weekday hours of 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM, holidays not skipped.
why: Going to a closed office plays the visit at its next opening (owner, Nov 1); only some clerks are full people with work spans, and an office with no record of hours must still have some, never none.
replacement: Every filing office's clerk or staff is a person with work spans (or the office's own published hours are a record), after which `data/office-hours.json` and this fallback are deleted.
